newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - British core inflation 2.7 percent in March.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - British core inflation 2.7 percent in March.

text.p: Britain's core inflation rate rose by 0.3 percent in March, bringing the annual figure to 2.7 percent, official figures showed on Thursday.
The figures were better than expected by economic analysts and provided a welcome boost for the ruling Conservative Party ahead of the May 1 election.

Prime Minister John Major, whose party is well behind the main opposition Labour Party in opinion polls, said Britain was enjoying the "longest period of low inflation for 50 years and I expect that to continue".
The monthly inflation rate in February was 0.4 percent, with core annual inflation standing at 2.9 percent.
The core inflation rate excludes mortgage payments and the government had been hoping to reduce the figure to 2.5 percent by the end of the current parliament.
Analysts said that although the target had been missed, an outcome of 2.7 percent would please the government.
Jeremy Hawkins of Bank of America said: "The government must be pretty pleased with today's numbers.
"They will use today's numbers, together with a strong employment report yesterday, to underline the generally strong performance we're seeing in the UK economy."
Stewart Robinson of London's Lombard Street Research said: "The government really couldn't hope for a much better economic backdrop."

The Conservatives, however, have struggled to persuade voters to pay attention to the party's campaign slogan that "Britain is booming". Instead, attention has focused on the party's splits over Europe.
But while financial markets generally welcomed the inflation data, some analysts felt that upward pressure on prices could resume soon as consumers continued to spend freely.
The Office of National Statistics said the inflation rate was helped by the largest March drop in seasonal food prices for 40 years.
